newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: BP Australia eyes Woolworths petrol profit.
newsitem.headline: BP Australia eyes Woolworths petrol profit.

text.p: Petrol marketing and refining group BP Australia Ltd said on Wednesday it was monitoring retailer Woolworths Ltd's recent move into the petrol retailing business in Australia.

"We believe they (Woolworths) are making, out of some of those country sites we have looked at, if you forget about overheads, returns of well above 20 percent," BP Australia's general manager reseller Gerry Houston told a press briefing.
Houston said operations by Woolworths and other independent petrol retailers were growing at rate which suggested it was attractive for them to invest in that market.

This contrasted markedly with the situation of Australia's four petrol refiners and marketers whose overall petrol retail operations made an average return of just 5.2 percent in calendar 1996, Houston said.

Houston referred to an independent report prepared for industry body, the Australian Institute of Petroleum, last month which found the industry's net profit totalled A$222 million in 1996, the lowest since the survey began in 1992.
Australia's eight refineries are run by the Royal Dutch/Shell Group, Mobil Corp, British Petroleum and Ampol Ltd, a joint venture between Caltex Australia Ltd and Pioneer International Ltd.
BP Australia, a unit of The British Petroleum Co Plc, has a 20 percent share of the retail market but made just a four percent return on its investment in 1996.
David Baldry, BP Australia's marketing director, said the industry wanted a level playing field for petrol retailing.
This could be achieved by deregulating the market or by scrapping the existing market legislation, he said.
Baldry said the refiners needed a freer hand to restructure their retail network of service stations in order to improve profitability to sustainable levels.

Current legislation restricts refiners to operating just five percent of their service stations and to a minimum nine year tenure period for station franchisees, restrictions not placed on independent retailers.
The Australian petrol retail market was one of the most competitive in the world, Baldry said.
Consequently the deregulation of the market was unlikely to to result in higher prices for consumers, he said.
Baldry said consumers were suspicious of large oil companies because of the weekly fluctuations of petrol prices at retail sites, a factor largely out of the control of the refiners.
"Research indicates it is not the price the consumer is worried about, it is the fact that the price is irregular," he said.
Baldry said BP Australia would be happy to make a return on its Australia petrol retail operations of about 12 percent, the average return of BP's retail operations world-wide.
